country_overview: Mexico operates a free-floating exchange-rate regime, set by the Comisión de Cambios — officials of the Secretaría de Hacienda y Crédito Público (SHCP) and Banco de México — under Article 21 of the Ley del Banco de México, with Banco de México as the central bank. Under Article 8 of the Ley Monetaria, foreign currency is not legal tender in Mexico and payment obligations denominated in foreign currency for fulfilment in Mexico are discharged in pesos at the prevailing exchange rate. Cross-border movements of cash by travellers are administered by the customs authorities under Article 9 of the Ley Aduanera, which requires a mandatory declaration when means of payment exceed the equivalent of USD 10,000. Banks separately apply anti-money-laundering controls and limits to certain US-dollar cash operations under Article 115 of the Ley de Instituciones de Crédito — a cash-handling measure, not an exchange control; the currently applicable thresholds and customer categories remain to be verified. No general Banco de México authorisation or approval requirement for holding or transferring currency was identified in the statutes reviewed for this phase; this is a bounded review finding, not a conclusion that no sectoral or capital-movement restriction exists. The customs, exchange-rate, AML and reporting regimes are kept distinct and are not conflated.

summary.traveler: Travellers entering or leaving Mexico must file a mandatory customs declaration when the cash, national or foreign checks, payment orders or other collectible instruments they carry — or a combination — exceed the equivalent of USD 10,000 in total (Ley Aduanera, Article 9). The duty is symmetric on entry and exit and is filed on the official form approved by the SAT; failure to declare carries a fine of 20% to 40% of the amount exceeding USD 10,000 (Article 185, fracción VII). This customs declaration is separate from the anti-money-laundering controls banks apply to US-dollar cash operations.
summary.business: Under Article 8 of the Ley Monetaria, obligations payable in Mexico that are denominated in foreign currency are discharged in pesos at the exchange rate prevailing on the payment date; foreign currency is not legal tender. Currency conversion and cross-border payments run through banks and other intermediaries authorised under Mexican law, and the exchange-rate regime is free-floating and set by the Comisión de Cambios. No general Banco de México authorisation or approval requirement for making cross-border payments or transferring funds was identified in the statutes reviewed for this phase — a bounded review finding, not a conclusion that no restriction exists. Banks separately apply anti-money-laundering controls to certain US-dollar cash operations under Article 115 of the Ley de Instituciones de Crédito.

rules.bring_foreign_currency_in: A traveller entering Mexico must file a mandatory customs declaration when the means of payment carried — cash, national or foreign checks, payment orders or any other collectible document, or a combination — exceed the equivalent of USD 10,000 in total (Ley Aduanera, Article 9), on the official form approved by the SAT. At or below that amount no declaration is required. The operational customs authority is the Agencia Nacional de Aduanas de México (ANAM). This customs declaration is distinct from the anti-money-laundering controls on US-dollar cash operations at banks.
rules.take_foreign_currency_out: A traveller leaving Mexico must likewise file a mandatory customs declaration when the means of payment carried exceed the equivalent of USD 10,000 in total (Ley Aduanera, Article 9); the obligation is symmetric with entry. No Banco de México permission or export limit on physically carrying currency out of the country was identified in the statutes reviewed for this phase; this is a bounded review finding, and the only monetary threshold on the traveller identified is the customs declaration duty. Anti-money-laundering controls apply separately to US-dollar cash operations conducted through banks.
rules.cash_declaration_threshold: The customs declaration threshold is means of payment — cash, national or foreign checks, payment orders or any other collectible document, or a combination — exceeding the equivalent of USD 10,000 in total, for a traveller entering or leaving the country (Ley Aduanera, Article 9). It is a mandatory report to the customs authorities (ANAM) on the SAT-approved form, triggered only above USD 10,000; failure to declare carries a fine of 20% to 40% of the excess (Article 185, fracción VII). This border declaration is separate from three other regimes: anti-money-laundering controls on US-dollar cash operations (Ley de Instituciones de Crédito, Article 115), UIF suspicious- and cash-transaction reporting, and the LFPIORPI domestic cash-payment limits.
rules.resident_holding_rules: No claim-matched primary source establishing a general Banco de México approval requirement for resident foreign-currency accounts was verified in this phase; equally, account eligibility and operation were not established by a claim-matched source and remain a verification target. Banks separately apply anti-money-laundering controls and limits to certain US-dollar cash operations under Article 115 of the Ley de Instituciones de Crédito and its implementing general provisions — the currently applicable thresholds and customer categories remain to be verified — alongside AML/KYC, tax and each institution's own conditions. This does not guarantee that any resident may open any particular account.
rules.non_resident_rules: Non-resident account eligibility, operation and repatriation rules were not established by a claim-matched source in this phase and remain verification targets. Anti-money-laundering controls and limits apply to certain US-dollar cash operations under Article 115 of the Ley de Instituciones de Crédito (thresholds and customer categories to be verified), and account opening remains subject to sanctions screening, AML/KYC, tax and each institution's requirements — regimes separate from the exchange-rate framework. There is no entitlement to any particular account or service.
rules.business_invoicing_settlement: Under Article 8 of the Ley Monetaria, obligations payable in Mexico that are denominated in foreign currency are discharged by delivering the peso equivalent at the exchange rate prevailing on the payment date (foreign currency is not legal tender), subject to the statute's exception for payments originating in funds transferred from abroad. Cross-border business payments and receipts run through banks and other intermediaries authorised under Mexican law; no general Banco de México authorisation requirement for ordinary cross-border payments was identified in the statutes reviewed for this phase (a bounded review finding). Anti-money-laundering controls (Ley de Instituciones de Crédito, Article 115) and reporting obligations apply. This does not establish an unrestricted choice of invoice currency, which depends on the contract and the Ley Monetaria settlement rule.
rules.exchange_controls: Mexico's foreign-exchange regime is free-floating and set by the Comisión de Cambios — the SHCP and Banco de México — under Article 21 of the Ley del Banco de México; the Comisión determines the exchange-rate regime and Banco de México sets the rules for determining the exchange rate (Ley Monetaria, Article 8). No general authorisation, permission or approval regime for buying, holding or transferring currency was identified in the foreign-exchange statutes reviewed for this phase; this is a bounded review finding, not a conclusion that no sectoral or capital-movement restriction exists. The operative restrictions identified are of a different character and are kept distinct — anti-money-laundering controls on US-dollar cash operations (Ley de Instituciones de Crédito, Article 115), the customs border declaration (Ley Aduanera, Article 9), and AML reporting. Whether any narrower sectoral or capital-movement restriction exists outside the statutes reviewed remains a verification target.
rules.banking_conversion_practicality: Currency conversion and cross-border payments in Mexico are provided through banks, and through casas de cambio and centros cambiarios authorised and supervised under Mexican law by the Comisión Nacional Bancaria y de Valores (CNBV) and Banco de México. These authorised intermediaries apply anti-money-laundering identification and controls on certain US-dollar cash operations under Article 115 of the Ley de Instituciones de Crédito (applicable thresholds and customer categories to be verified); authorisation does not guarantee that any particular institution offers a given currency, service or price.

disclaimer: This page provides general informational reference only. Foreign-exchange, customs and anti-money-laundering rules in Mexico are set by the Ley Monetaria, the Ley del Banco de México, the Ley Aduanera, the Ley de Instituciones de Crédito and related regulations, and may change; requirements depend on residency, the transaction type and amount, documentation, and the applicable Banco de México, SHCP, CNBV, ANAM and UIF framework. This is not legal, regulatory, tax, financial, or compliance advice. Always verify current rules directly with Banco de México, the customs authority (ANAM), or a qualified professional before making any financial or travel decisions.
